Volume 05 · Chapter 04

Competitive equilibrium and surplus

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c03

By the endSolve partial equilibrium and distinguish efficiency from distribution.

Connect individual choices to a market outcome

Capability: construct and solve a competitive partial-equilibrium model, calculate the incidence and welfare effects of an intervention, and distinguish efficiency from distribution. Prerequisites: firm choice and costs, consumer welfare and duality, and the differentiation and integration tools from Volume 2.

A government charges a fee on each unit sold. The seller sends the payment, but buyers may face a higher price and sellers may receive less after the fee. Who loses, how much revenue is collected, and which trades disappear? Those are three different questions. Answer them by specifying behavior on both sides, clearing the market, and accounting for the gains and costs of the resulting allocation.

All numerical cases in this chapter are original hypothetical economies. Unless stated otherwise, quantities are units per week, prices and specific taxes are dollars per unit, and benefits, costs, profits and tax revenue are dollars per week. The market is competitive: each buyer and seller treats the price as given when choosing. This is a behavioral assumption, not a conclusion obtained merely by counting firms. Products have a common defined quality; information, enforcement and trading opportunities are specified rather than inferred from a curve.

Aggregate quantities at the same price

Let di(p) be buyer i's demand holding that buyer's income and other relevant prices fixed. Let sj(p) be firm j's optimal output holding technology and input prices fixed. Market demand and supply are D(p) = Σidi(p) and S(p) = Σjsj(p). This is horizontal aggregation: add quantities at a common price, not prices at a common quantity. Respect zero-demand and shutdown branches before adding. If individual choices are correspondences, aggregate the feasible combinations of their choices; a single arbitrarily selected branch can miss an equilibrium.

Partial equilibrium treats the relevant background incomes, other prices and technologies as fixed, or supplies a reason their feedback can be ignored. The number of firms is fixed for the short-run supply curve here. Long-run entry changes that number. A wage increase affecting all producers shifts their cost schedules; a higher output price on an unchanged cost schedule moves their chosen quantities along supply. A change in income can shift demand, whereas a change in this good's price moves along a demand schedule defined at fixed income.

An untaxed equilibrium consists of a common price p* and individual optimal choices whose total purchases equal total sales: D(p*) = S(p*) = Q*. Equalities between two drawn curves represent an economic equilibrium only if those curves describe feasible optimizing choices under the same assumptions. A firm with market power does not generally choose output by setting price equal to marginal cost.

Here is a useful sufficient existence result. If D and S are continuous on a price interval [a,b], and excess demand z(p) = D(p) − S(p) satisfies z(a) ≥ 0 and z(b) ≤ 0, the intermediate value theorem gives a clearing price. If z is strictly decreasing, that price is unique: two roots with p1 < p2 would imply 0 = z(p1) > z(p2) = 0. Downward demand and upward supply with at least one strictly monotone provide this condition. These are sufficient conditions, not universal properties of consumer demand or technologies.

A zero-trade boundary deserves explicit attention. If the highest willingness to pay is below the lowest avoidable unit cost, positive trade is inefficient and the clearing price can be an interval supporting Q = 0. Discrete choices may instead require correspondences or rationing and need not admit a clearing price under a proposed single-valued rule. Do not extend a linear equation to negative purchases or production just to manufacture a crossing.

For a smooth demand shifter a, differentiate D(p(a),a) = S(p(a)) at an interior equilibrium:

[Dp − S′]p′(a) + Da = 0,
p′(a) = Da/(S′ − Dp),   Q′(a) = S′p′(a).

Thus a positive demand shift raises price and quantity when Dp < 0 and S′ > 0. This compares equilibria. It does not prove that a real adjustment process converges to one, or tell how quickly firms enter. Nor do two observed price–quantity pairs identify a demand curve: both schedules can move between observations.

MIT's 14.01 Lecture 9 handout supplies graphical benchmarks for market clearing, shifts and the consumer/producer-surplus areas. The existence conditions and original algebra here make explicit which smooth partial-equilibrium case is being analyzed.

What the surplus areas measure

Under quasilinear preferences ui(qi,zi) = fi(qi) + zi, with the numeraire price equal to one, a buyer's choice maximizes fi(qi) − pqi. This reduction assumes the numeraire constraint does not bind throughout the comparison, or that unrestricted numeraire transfers are feasible. Normalize fi(0) = 0. The marginal benefit f′i is measured in dollars per unit. With concave benefits, allocating units to their highest marginal values yields an aggregate benefit B(Q) and inverse demand PD(Q) = B′(Q) on a differentiable branch.

Similarly, let C(Q) be the least aggregate variable cost of producing Q among the existing firms, with C(0) = 0. With convex variable costs and an efficient allocation of production, its derivative is inverse supply PS(Q). Let F denote the existing firms' total committed fixed cost over this comparison. For actual efficient trade Q at buyer price pb and seller receipt ps, define

CS = B(Q) − pbQ = ∫0QPD(x) dx − pbQ,
PS = psQ − C(Q) = psQ − ∫0QPS(x) dx,
economic profit = PS − F.

These integrals require the stated marginal-benefit and marginal-cost interpretation. A supply branch with an avoidable startup fee is not generally enough to recover total cost by integrating from zero: the fee must be added and the decision to operate evaluated. Likewise, PS is not revenue, and short-run PS need not equal profit. Opportunity costs, including the owners' alternatives, belong in economic cost.

Without taxes, CS + PS = B(Q) − C(Q). Transaction payments cancel because the buyer's expense is the seller's receipt. If committed F is unchanged, maximizing this surplus is equivalent to maximizing B − C − F. Its derivative is PD − PS; with decreasing marginal benefit and increasing marginal cost, the competitive crossing maximizes the total. For Q below Q*, the omitted marginal trades have benefit above cost; beyond Q*, extra units cost more than their benefit. Integrating that difference proves the welfare loss, including boundary optima when there is no positive crossing.

Efficient allocation among people and firms matters as well as total Q. For concave fi, convex Cj and interior positive individual choices, optimal allocation makes all active marginal benefits and all active marginal costs equal to the common price. Otherwise moving a small quantity from a lower-value buyer to a higher-value buyer, or from a higher-cost producer to a lower-cost producer, raises total surplus. Boundary inequalities replace equalities for inactive participants. These statements concern the specified one-market allocation, with no external costs, missing benefits or unmodeled feedback.

The quasilinear surplus decomposition also appears in the preference setup of MIT 14.581 Lecture 24, slides 10–12. Only that setup is used here; its trade-policy game is a separate model. With income effects, the ordinary demand area is generally not an exact money measure of welfare: use the compensated expenditure comparisons established in Chapter 2.

Adding dollars is also a distributional choice. A $10 gain to one group offsets a $10 loss to another in total surplus even if their incomes and social priorities differ. A Pareto improvement makes everyone weakly better off and someone strictly better off. A positive total gain may allow compensation under feasible quasilinear transfers; it does not mean compensation actually occurs. Report winners, losers and the transfer mechanism separately. A weighted social objective or an externality can rank policies differently from the unweighted private-surplus calculation.

Solve the tax wedge before assigning its burden

A specific tax t ≥ 0 per traded unit creates pb − ps = t. At positive trade, market clearing becomes D(ps + t) = S(ps). Under full compliance, the same effective tax base, unchanged enforcement and transaction costs, flexible prices and identical perceived incentives, assigning legal remittance to buyers or sellers leaves these two equations unchanged. That is the precise basis for remittance invariance. Different evasion opportunities, salience, price controls, bargaining or compliance costs can invalidate the comparison.

To derive local incidence, differentiate the clearing equation along a smooth interior equilibrium:

D′(pb)(dps/dt + 1) = S′(ps)dps/dt,
dpb/dt = S′/(S′ − D′),   dps/dt = D′/(S′ − D′),
dQ/dt = D′S′/(S′ − D′).

For D′ < 0 and S′ > 0, buyer price rises, seller receipt falls, and trade shrinks. At an initially untaxed positive-price equilibrium, define the positive demand-elasticity magnitude εD = −D′p/Q and supply elasticity εS = S′p/Q. The common p/Q cancels:

marginal buyer share = εS/(εD + εS),
marginal seller share = εD/(εD + εS).

The less price-responsive side bears more of the per-unit price wedge. These shares describe price changes, not each group's entire welfare loss; reduced trading opportunities matter too. At an existing tax pb differs from ps, so elasticities evaluated using their own prices do not share a common normalization. Use the derivative formula directly or retain the separate price factors. For a finite tax with nonlinear curves, solve the new equilibrium or integrate the changing derivatives; an initial point elasticity alone is not an exact finite-change formula.

Frank Levy's MIT tax-incidence note presents the wedge and matched demand/supply changes. The derivation above states the differential scope explicitly. If supply is locally perfectly elastic, buyers bear the full marginal tax; if supply is locally perfectly inelastic and demand responds normally, sellers bear it. With perfectly inelastic demand and responsive supply, buyers bear it. If both quantities are fixed or the equilibrium is at a kink, the smooth unique-derivative calculation may fail.

Tax revenue is R = tQ. If it is retained within the measured economy and valued dollar for dollar, adding it back gives CS + PS + R = B(Q) − C(Q). This accounting counts transfers once and excludes any separate public-service benefit or collection cost. With an initially efficient market and unchanged F, deadweight loss is

DWL = ∫QtQ*[PD(x) − PS(x)] dx.

For linear inverse curves PD = a − bx and PS = c + dx, with a > c and b,d > 0, Q* = (a − c)/(b + d) and Qt = (a − c − t)/(b + d) while 0 ≤ t < a − c. Therefore DWL = t(Q* − Qt)/2 = t²/[2(b + d)]. The triangular formula is exact here. At t ≥ a − c, trade is zero and the loss equals all initial gains from trade; the interior formula must not be extended to negative Q. For smooth nonlinear curves, the small-tax triangle is an approximation. A tax correcting an externality or another preexisting distortion can have a different net welfare effect.

Worked example 1: a market, a tax and a complete welfare ledger

Two buyer groups demand DA(p) = max(0,120 − 4p) and DB(p) = max(0,60 − 2p). Two producer groups supply SA(p) = max(0,p − 6) and SB(p) = max(0,2p − 12). Their common demand choke price is 30 and supply starts at 6. On the active branch, D = 180 − 6p and S = 3p − 18.

Clear the market: 180 − 6p = 3p − 18 gives p* = 22 and Q* = 48. Both groups participate: buyer quantities are 32 and 16; producer quantities are 16 and 32. Inverse demand is 30 − Q/6; inverse supply is 6 + Q/3. Under the quasilinear efficient-allocation conditions, CS = (30 − 22)48/2 = 192 and PS = (22 − 6)48/2 = 384. Total gains are 576. If committed fixed cost is 60, total profit is 324, and surplus net of that committed cost is 516.

Now set t = 6. Solving 180 − 6(ps + 6) = 3ps − 18 yields ps = 18, pb = 24 and Qt = 36. Buyers pay 2 more per unit and sellers receive 4 less. Initial elasticities are εD = 6(22)/48 = 11/4 and εS = 3(22)/48 = 11/8; the resulting buyer share 1/3 agrees with the finite answer because these active curves are linear.

Weekly welfare ledger; fixed cost unchanged
AccountNo taxTax t = 6Change
Consumer surplus192(30 − 24)36/2 = 108−84
Producer surplus384(18 − 6)36/2 = 216−168
Tax revenue06 × 36 = 216+216
CS + PS + revenue576540−36

The welfare loss is 36, also 6(48 − 36)/2. Government revenue is not itself that loss. Independently, B(36) = 30(36) − 36²/12 = 972 and C(36) = 6(36) + 36²/6 = 432, giving B − C = 540. Profit after the tax is 216 − 60 = 156. All comparisons subtracting the unchanged 60 yield the same loss of 36.

For a general interior t, ps = 22 − 2t/3, pb = 22 + t/3, Qt = 48 − 2t and R = 48t − 2t². Revenue peaks at t = 12 with Q = 24 and R = 288; this is a revenue objective, not a welfare optimum. At t = 24 trade vanishes. For higher taxes use Q = 0; without transactions, supporting price quotes need not be unique.

Entry changes the relevant supply response

Suppose potential entrants are identical, can adopt the same technology, face constant input prices as the industry expands, and can enter or exit without additional barriers or unrecovered setup obligations. Let CLR(q) include every avoidable long-run economic cost of an active firm. If a positive-output competitive equilibrium permits unrestricted entry, positive profits invite further entry, while negative profits make exit preferable. In the ideal divisible-entry model, an active firm therefore earns zero economic profit.

At a smooth interior optimal scale q*, profit maximization gives p = C′LR(q*) and zero profit gives p = CLR(q*)/q*. Thus marginal cost equals average cost. Differentiating average cost shows why: AC′(q) = [qC′(q) − C(q)]/q². The competitive entry price is the global minimum of AC, when that minimum is attained. A stationary point alone is insufficient. At this price, optimal firm scale and the number of active firms together supply market demand.

The conventional entry/exit mechanism and constant-, increasing- and decreasing-cost industry distinction are introduced in OpenStax's long-run entry section. The constant-input-price and common-technology assumptions above support a horizontal long-run supply relation: demand changes are accommodated by the number of firms at the same minimum average cost. This does not require each active firm's technology to exhibit constant returns at every output.

If expansion raises scarce input prices, shifts technology, or draws in firms with different costs, horizontal long-run supply and universal zero profits do not follow. Low-cost incumbents can earn scarcity rents. Zero economic profit already compensates the opportunity costs of labor and capital; it does not imply no cash income. Entry adjustment can take time, so an empirical tax-incidence estimate needs a stated horizon.

Worked example 2: short-run profits and long-run scale

Each active firm has long-run cost C(q) = 16 + 4q + q² for q > 0 and can exit at cost zero. AC(q) = 16/q + 4 + q. Its derivative is 1 − 16/q², negative below q = 4 and positive above. Therefore the global minimum occurs at q* = 4 with AC = MC = 12. Demand D(p) = max(0,120 − 5p) gives Q = 60 at p = 12, supplied by n = 15 identical firms, each earning 12(4) − 16 − 16 − 16 = 0.

Demand now becomes max(0,144 − 5p). Initially there are still 15 firms and their fixed charges are committed. Each chooses q = (p − 4)/2 on its active short-run branch. Clearing 144 − 5p = 15(p − 4)/2 gives p = 348/25 = 13.92, q = 124/25 = 4.96 and Q = 74.4. Each firm's profit is q² − 16 = 5,376/625 = 8.6016. The identity follows from p = 4 + 2q: pq − (16 + 4q + q²) = q² − 16.

With entry and unchanged technology/input prices, the long-run price returns to 12. Demand is now 84, served by 21 firms producing four each. Quantity increases further, profits return to zero, and the original 15 firms reduce their individual output relative to the short-run peak. This is a comparative-static endpoint, not a dated forecast of entry.

Divisibility matters. If demand were 122 − 5p, the price 12 would require 62 units, or 15.5 firms at efficient scale. With indivisible identical firms, there is no integer n delivering that exact zero-profit competitive configuration. With 15 active firms, price clears at 304/25 = 12.16 and per-firm profit is 404/625 > 0; with 16, price is 154/13 and per-firm profit is −103/169. A finite entry model must specify how entrants anticipate the price change. Rounding 15.5 without reconsidering incentives does not solve that different model.

A controlled price does not specify who trades

A binding price ceiling below the competitive price typically produces D(p̄) > S(p̄). If all willing supply trades, Q = S(p̄), but that quantity alone does not identify consumer surplus. Are units allocated to the highest-value buyers, by lottery, through queues, or through resale? Queueing consumes resources; resale can alter both allocation and who receives rents. The usual demand-area calculation up to Q assumes the highest-value units are the ones consumed. A random allocation can generate an additional loss at the same price and quantity.

A binding price floor similarly leaves intended supply above demand unless another buyer, such as a government, purchases the difference. State actual output, purchases, disposal and fiscal costs before calculating welfare. Apply the model's equations to the actual trading rule, rather than labeling an uncleared price–quantity pair a competitive equilibrium.

Exercises

  1. Aggregation with a kink. D1(p) = max(0,40 − 2p), D2(p) = max(0,30 − p), and S(p) = max(0,2p − 10), with p ≥ 0. Write the piecewise market demand; solve the equilibrium and its CS and PS under the surplus assumptions. Then replace supply by max(0,2p − 50). Solve again and explain why using both demand branches beyond their choke prices fails.
  2. Existence, uniqueness and no trade. Prove the stated uniqueness result from strict decrease of excess demand. For D(p) = max(0,12 − p) and S(p) = max(0,p − 15), identify every nonnegative clearing price. Does uniqueness of the quantity imply uniqueness of the price? Identify the missing hypothesis.
  3. A complete tax calculation. In Worked example 1, set t = 9. Calculate both prices, quantity, CS, PS, revenue and deadweight loss. Compare the surplus losses with revenue. State what changes if t = 27, and whether remitting the same compliant tax through buyers changes the result.
  4. Local incidence and limiting cases. At an untaxed equilibrium p = 20, Q = 100, let εD = 1/2 and εS = 3/2. Derive the approximate changes in both prices and quantity from a small tax t = 2. Explain why these are only first-order approximations without additional functional assumptions. What happens to local incidence when supply is perfectly elastic? When it is perfectly inelastic?
  5. Entry and avoidable costs. Identical potential firms have C(q) = 25 + 2q + q² when active and zero cost on exit. Market demand is max(0,170 − 10p). Find the long-run scale, entry price, total quantity and number of firms. Repeat if the active fixed cost rises to 36, with the same marginal-cost schedule. Explain why unchanged marginal cost does not keep the long-run price fixed.
  6. Allocation under a ceiling. In Worked example 1, impose p̄ = 18 and suppose all willing supply trades. Calculate demand, supply, shortage and total surplus if the highest-value buyers receive the units. Now interpret demand as a continuum of one-unit buyers ranked by reservation value. Allocate the available units uniformly by lottery among all buyers willing to pay 18; each has the same probability of service. Compute expected total benefit and surplus, and separate the loss from reduced trade from the additional allocation loss. Ignore queueing and administrative costs.
  7. Do the data identify demand? A market moves from (p,Q) = (20,60) to (22,66). An analyst reports demand elasticity +1 from the two percentage changes. Construct a pair of downward-sloping demand curves and a fixed upward supply curve consistent with both observations. Explain the identification failure and propose the type of additional variation and evidence needed to estimate a demand response.
  8. Efficiency and distribution. A proposed change gives group A a money-equivalent gain of 90 and group B a loss of 60, under quasilinear preferences with feasible costless transfers. Is it a Pareto improvement as proposed? What transfers from A to B could make both weakly better off and one strictly better off? Compare the unweighted change with a social objective giving B twice A's weight. Separately, suppose the change also creates an omitted external loss of 40. What happens to the unweighted net gain?
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. For 0 ≤ p ≤ 20, D = 70 − 3p; for 20 ≤ p ≤ 30, D = 30 − p; for p ≥ 30, D = 0. At the joining prices the formulas agree. The original active supply crosses the first branch: 70 − 3p = 2p − 10 gives p = 16, Q = 22, with demands 8 and 14. CS is the sum of individual areas: (20 − 16)8/2 + (30 − 16)14/2 = 16 + 98 = 114. PS = (16 − 5)22/2 = 121. Total surplus is 235.

    For new supply, production begins only above 25. Thus the active demand branch is D = 30 − p, and 30 − p = 2p − 50 gives p = 80/3 and Q = 10/3. Buyer group 1 demands zero. New CS = (30 − 80/3)(10/3)/2 = 50/9 and PS = (80/3 − 25)(10/3)/2 = 25/9, for total surplus 25/3. Blindly solving 70 − 3p = 2p − 50 gives p = 24, outside the first demand branch and below the supply threshold; it is not an equilibrium. Even when the candidate is invalid, the branch restrictions identify the correct equation.

  2. If p1 < p2 were both roots of a strictly decreasing z, then z(p1) > z(p2), contradicting their common value zero. In the specified market, every p in [12,15] produces D = S = 0. Below 12 there is positive demand and zero supply; above 15 there is positive supply and zero demand. Hence quantity is uniquely zero, but price is an interval. Excess demand is flat at zero on that interval, so the strict-decrease hypothesis is absent. Economically, no mutually beneficial positive trade exists between the willingness-to-pay ceiling 12 and entry cost threshold 15.

  3. ps = 22 − 2(9)/3 = 16, pb = 25, Q = 30. CS = (30 − 25)30/2 = 75; PS = (16 − 6)30/2 = 150; R = 9(30) = 270. Their sum is 495, so DWL = 576 − 495 = 81, also 9(48 − 30)/2. Consumer loss is 192 − 75 = 117 and producer-surplus loss is 384 − 150 = 234. Together they lose 351; revenue recovers 270, leaving 81. With t = 27, no positive trade is feasible because the tax exceeds the maximum initial benefit–cost gap of 24. Thus Q = R = CS = PS = 0 and all 576 initial variable gains are lost; unchanged committed fixed costs cancel in the comparison. Price quotes need not be unique, and the interior formulas' negative output is invalid. Remittance through buyers gives the same allocation under the assumptions stated in the chapter.

  4. The buyer share is (3/2)/(1/2 + 3/2) = 3/4; the seller share is 1/4. Thus Δpb ≈ 1.5 and Δps ≈ −0.5. Recover slopes from elasticity: D′ = −(1/2)100/20 = −2.5 and S′ = (3/2)100/20 = 7.5. Both sides give ΔQ ≈ −2.5(1.5) = 7.5(−0.5) = −3.75, so Q ≈ 96.25. The supplied elasticities describe the initial point; nonlinear slopes can change over the finite move. Linear schedules over the relevant range would make these changes exact. With a horizontal supply price, seller receipt stays fixed and buyers bear the tax; with fixed supplied quantity and downward demand, buyer price stays fixed and sellers bear it, as long as those branches remain feasible.

  5. Initially AC = 25/q + 2 + q and AC′ = 1 − 25/q². The unique global minimum is q = 5, with p = AC = MC = 12. Demand is Q = 170 − 120 = 50, so n = 10. With fixed cost 36, AC = 36/q + 2 + q, minimized at q = 6 with p = 14. Demand is Q = 30, served by n = 5. Cost and revenue both equal 84 per active firm in the second configuration. The marginal-cost function 2 + 2q is unchanged, but the efficient scale moves and the firm must cover the larger avoidable fixed cost. A price of 12 would leave the entrant's maximized profit negative after that cost. These exact integer configurations avoid the indivisibility issue discussed in the example.

  6. Demand is 180 − 6(18) = 72, supply is 3(18) − 18 = 36, and shortage is 36. With efficient allocation of these 36 units, benefit is B(36) = 972 and variable cost is C(36) = 432, so total surplus is 540. CS is 972 − 18(36) = 324 and PS is 18(36) − 432 = 216. Relative to 576 initially, reduced trade loses 36.

    Under the stated lottery, each of 72 willing one-unit buyers receives service with probability 36/72 = 1/2. The sum of their reservation values is B(72) = 30(72) − 72²/12 = 1,728. Expected consumed benefit is half of that, 864. Cost remains 432, so expected surplus is 432, with expected CS = 864 − 648 = 216 and PS = 216. The total loss is 144: 36 from reduced trade plus 972 − 864 = 108 from misallocation at the same quantity. Payments do not change that total. The lottery calculation requires this specified allocation rule; price and shortage alone do not imply it.

  7. A valid construction is S(p) = 3p, initial D0(p) = max(0,100 − 2p), and later D1(p) = max(0,110 − 2p). They clear at (20,60) and (22,66), respectively. Each demand slope is −2; the observed positive relationship arises from a demand shift and movement along supply. The analyst's calculation (6/60)/(2/20) = +1 is arithmetically correct but is not a demand elasticity. A credible supply shifter excluded from demand could help trace demand, provided its relevance, exogeneity and exclusion conditions are justified. Randomized effective prices may answer a suitably scoped demand question if interference and selection are handled. Full credit requires a distinction between movement along a fixed schedule and changes in that schedule, plus an explicit identifying assumption; merely adding observations or naming an instrument is insufficient.

  8. The proposed allocation is not a Pareto improvement because B loses 60. If A transfers T to B, their net changes are 90 − T and −60 + T. Both are nonnegative for 60 ≤ T ≤ 90; since their sum remains 30, at least one is strictly positive throughout that interval. Feasibility and actual execution of the transfer matter. Without the transfer, unweighted gain is 90 − 60 = 30, whereas the proposed weighted objective changes by 90 − 2(60) = −30. These are different welfare criteria. In the separate omitted-external-loss scenario, the unweighted net change is 30 − 40 = −10. Full credit distinguishes a feasible compensation opportunity, a delivered Pareto improvement and the stated social criterion; it does not declare one ranking uniquely mandated by the arithmetic.

Teach-back and delayed transfer

Teach-back: use one diagram or a small numerical table to explain why the remitting side need not bear a tax, why tax revenue differs from deadweight loss, and why total surplus does not certify a Pareto improvement. Define the two prices and actual traded quantity before shading or calculating any area. A successful explanation includes the model assumptions and an example of an allocation or externality that would change the welfare calculation.

Delayed check: after several days, solve D(p) = max(0,60 − 2p), S(p) = max(0,p − 6) first without tax and then with t = 3. Give the welfare loss under the chapter's exact-surplus assumptions and one reason a price ceiling would require more information.

Delayed-check answer

Without tax, p = 22 and Q = 16. With tax, 60 − 2(ps + 3) = ps − 6 gives ps = 20, pb = 23 and Q = 14. The loss is 3(16 − 14)/2 = 3. Initial CS = 64 and PS = 128; afterward CS = 49, PS = 98 and revenue = 42, giving 189 instead of 192. A ceiling also needs a rule assigning scarce units to buyers, and any queueing or enforcement costs, before total welfare can be calculated.

Next: general equilibrium and welfare connects multiple markets, endowments and firm ownership, then states the welfare theorems at their proper scope. The present calculations establish conditional one-market results and teach how to recognize when their assumptions are insufficient.

Sources and further study

  • Jonathan Gruber — MIT 14.01 Lecture 9 handout: market equilibrium and consumer/producer surplus, Fall 2023 — Primary graphical teaching reference for clearing, shifts and consumer/producer-surplus areas; original algebra and existence conditions are supplied in the chapter.
  • MIT 14.581 International Economics I — Lecture 24: Trade Policy Theory (II), Spring 2013, slides 10–12 — Scoped primary reference for quasilinear preferences, numeraire normalization, income/transfer plus surplus decomposition, and a partial-equilibrium interpretation.
  • Frank Levy — A Note on the Tax Incidence Problem, MIT 11.203, 19 September 2010 — Primary route for the buyer/seller price wedge and matched quantity changes underlying tax incidence.
  • OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e — 8.3 Entry and Exit Decisions in the Long Run — Primary open-textbook method route for competitive entry/exit and constant-, increasing- and decreasing-cost industries.
